analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin's manufacturer price at $20 per 1,000 units nationwide.
analysis.headline: The Insulin for All Act was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap the price drug manufacturers can charge for insulin at $20 per 1,000 units, in any form — vial, pen, or cartridge. Unlike the insulin price cap Congress actually passed in 2022, which applies only to people on Medicare, this cap would cover everyone in the country, including the millions of uninsured and privately insured people who pay the full manufacturer price. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8.4 million Americans who use insulin, especially uninsured people and those with high deductibles or copays who pay cash or full price for it. Unlike the existing Medicare insulin cap, this price limit would apply to the manufacturer price nationwide, lowering the starting cost for everyone regardless of insurance.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the manufacturer price of any insulin licensed and marketed in the United States at $20 per 1,000 units, covering vials, pens, cartridges, and other delivery forms.

Applies to the whole market, not just Medicare — unlike the 2022 law that capped insulin copays only for Medicare beneficiaries, this would lower the underlying manufacturer price for uninsured and privately insured people too.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers — Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Sanofi, whose list prices have historically run hundreds of dollars per vial — would absorb the gap between current prices and the $20 cap. If manufacturers cut supply or slowed new insulin investment rather than absorb it, patients could face shortages or fewer new products.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies to manufacturer prices only; it does not directly regulate pharmacy benefit managers or insurers, so middlemen could keep some of the savings instead of passing them to patients at the counter.

A statutory price ceiling this far below list prices — insulin has sold for $300 or more per vial — could lead manufacturers to limit supply, exit certain formulations, or slow development of new insulins, which would hurt the very patients the bill protects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of insulin users who pay cash prices or high deductibles, a $20 cap would be life-changing — insulin rationing because of cost is well documented. The main honest objections are that the bill only reaches manufacturers (not the middlemen who set what patients actually pay at the pharmacy) and that a hard price ceiling risks supply and future insulin innovation. Whether those risks outweigh the benefit is debatable; the bill never got far enough for the debate to happen.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Cori Bush introduced the Insulin for All Act of 2023 on March 9, 2023, with 13 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers keep charging their existing list prices, and middlemen in the drug pricing chain keep their current margins, because the price cap never advanced. Insulin users without insurance or with high cost-sharing gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Cori Bush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: 19 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House majority party in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with a Republican majority and the bill having no Republican cosponsors, it had no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and a Republican-controlled committee and House never acted on it.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill would cap their manufacturer price at $20 per 1,000 units, far below current list prices that can exceed $300 per vial. Their financial interest in keeping prices high ran directly against patients' need for affordable insulin.
A lower manufacturer price would shrink the spread and rebates these middlemen can capture on insulin. The bill does not directly regulate them, but cheaper insulin upstream cuts into their role.
